newsitem.title: UK: Sinn Fein expected to meet British officials.
newsitem.headline: Sinn Fein expected to meet British officials.

text.p: Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army (IRA), is expected to meet British officials on Wednesday for the first time since republican guerrillas ended a truce in February 1996, political sources said on Tuesday.

They said Sinn Fein politicians and British civil servants would hold talks in Belfast after Britain's new prime minister Tony Blair eased a ban on contacts last week in a bid to galvanise stalled efforts to bring peace to Northern Ireland.

An outlawed pro-British Protestant militia warned Blair against watering down conditions for Sinn Fein's entry to multi-party peace talks on the future of the British-ruled province, which are due to resume on June 3 after a break in the lead-up to British general elections held on May 1.
The Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF) said London must not "distort the (peace) process to the advantage of republicans" by relaxing a demand for a new, full IRA ceasefire.
"If the IRA fail to bring their campaign to an end they run the risk of pulling our society back into bloody conflict," the UFF said in a statement to a media outlet in Belfast.
Sinn Fein, which won two seats in the British parliament at the May 1 election, is banned from the peace negotiations until the IRA renews its ceasefire.
The IRA, fighting to end British rule in Northern Ireland and unite the province with the Irish Republic, broke a 17-month truce in February last year with a series of bombs in mainland Britain.

The UFF and other extremist groups, which have killed nationalist Roman Catholics in a campaign to thwart the IRA, have operated a ceasefire since October 1994. But it has become increasingly shaky in recent months because of IRA violence.

Sinn Fein's delegation to a meeting with British officials is likely to be led by Martin McGuinness, its chief negotiator who won a seat in the British parliament along with party president Gerry Adams.
Adams called on Tuesday for a British promise of direct entry to peace talks for Sinn Fein if the IRA abandoned violence.
He told the nationalist Irish News daily that if Britain gave clear assurances about viable all-party negotiations, Northern Ireland's floundering peace process could be restored.
Britain "should state clearly that Sinn Fein will join the negotiations immediately following an unequivocal restoration of the IRA", he said.
Adams criticised Blair for strongly defending Northern Ireland's union with Britain but he also signalled his belief that any fresh IRA ceasefire would be unequivocal.
Blair pledged that the province would remain part of the United Kingdom while a majority in the province supported it.
Northern Ireland's 60 percent Protestant majority want to stay British but the 40 percent Catholics, some of whom support the IRA, want a united Ireland freed of London's influence.
